description: Very interested in Scratch and love making fun and creative projects. Excited to join the “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer” challenge.
summary: Mars Outpost is a free browser game for kids aged 7 to 12. The player is a junior astronaut, alone on a Mars base, who must stay alive until a rescue ship lands. The player walks between rooms and uses stations: give battery packs to systems, clean dusty solar panels, melt ice for water, grow food, and hide from radiation in a shelter. Every choice has a cost, and time passes only when the player sleeps, so the player must plan like a real mission team. A friendly AI outpost computer talks with the player by voice or text, gives hints, and tells real NASA stories when they fit the moment. The events come from real NASA data, for example the solar storm of September 2017 that doubled the radiation that Curiosity measured on Mars, and the 2018 dust storm that ended the Opportunity mission. The game adapts to the player: a careful player gets harder events, and a new player gets more help. When the player fails, they try again from the last save and know why they failed. This makes the game a safe place to practise the decisions of a real astronaut, again and again.
details:
Play it: https://scratch.adaschools.com/play.html#10

The first load takes about 30 seconds. Click the green flag, then press SPACE to read the story cards. Walk with the arrow keys or WASD, and press SPACE at a station. Turn on the sound to hear the computer.

What it does:

- The player runs a Mars outpost with five resources: power (battery packs), water, food, oxygen and radiation dose.

- The base has rooms with stations. Each station is a short task with a real trade-off. A pack that runs the heater does not run the ice melter.

- Sols pass only when the player sleeps. The sleep screen shows each resource now and after the sleep, so the player plans before time moves.

- An event director starts a dust storm, a broken sensor or a solar storm, based on how well the player is doing. So each game is different.

- When the player fails, "Try again" starts from the last save. Failure is a lesson, not a punishment.

- The outpost computer is an AI character with a voice. It sees the same state as the game and gives hints that get clearer when the player is stuck. The game owns all numbers, so the AI cannot change a rule or make up a wrong fact.

Why it is a good way for a kid to learn:

- Replayable: every game is different, and kids use the same facts again in each game, so they remember them longer.

- Hard but fair: the challenge stays a little above the player's skill.

- Productive failure: the player sees why they failed, then tries again.

- We tested the balance with a simulator over 500 games: a careful player wins 92% of games, a careless player wins 8%, and a player who does nothing never wins. So good decisions matter.

What the player learns:

- Dust on solar panels can end a mission (Opportunity, 2018).

- A storm from the Sun can double the radiation on Mars in one day (Curiosity, September 2017).

- Astronauts must recycle water and make oxygen and food on Mars, because help from Earth is about 200 days away.

How we built it:

- The game is a Scratch 3 project, so other kids can open it, read the code and learn from it.

- We used our own Scratch-based editor, so our whole team could edit the same project at the same time.

- A small server (TypeScript, Node.js) runs the AI computer through OpenRouter, speech to text, and text to speech.

- All art is our own vector art in a clean sci-fi style. The music and sound effects are free CC0 files.

- The game plays in a web browser with no download and no account.

Team ThamMarvelTen, Bangkok.
